U.S. Moves to Remove South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA Trade Preference Starting 2027

03 Nov 2026, 03:18 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily World Desk · Source: www.dw.com

Image: dw.com · Photo source · Resized and letterboxed to 16:9; no AI generation

Share this article
WhatsAppFacebookTelegram
Key takeaways Overview The United States announced that it intends to terminate the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade‑preference status for South Africa and Rwanda beginning in January 2027. The decision was communicated by U.S. Trade Representative **Jamieson Greer**

Overview

The United States announced that it intends to terminate the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade‑preference status for South Africa and Rwanda beginning in January 2027. The decision was communicated by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Monday, citing “practices that are inconsistent with AGOA’s eligibility criteria.”

Confirmed Details

  • Decision timeline: Termination to take effect in January 2027.
  • Program background: AGOA, launched in 2000, grants duty‑free access to the U.S. market for over 1,800 products from 30+ sub‑Saharan African countries.
  • Current beneficiaries: South Africa is AGOA’s largest exporter, sending roughly $1.7 billion of goods (e.g., auto parts, citrus, wine) to the United States in 2025.
  • Official statements:
  • Greer said the governments of Rwanda and South Africa are “engaging in practices that undermine American trade and investment and pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign‑policy interests.”
  • The South African Trade Ministry noted that AGOA accounts for about 10 % of its U.S. exports and 1 % of its total global exports.

Reported Reasons (Unspecified)

The U.S. statement did not list concrete examples of the alleged barriers or security concerns. Media reports link the Rwanda action to recent U.S. sanctions over alleged support for the M23 rebel group in the Democratic Republic of Congo, but the AGOA notice itself only references “practices inconsistent with eligibility criteria.”

Reactions from Affected Countries

  • South Africa: The Trade Ministry called AGOA “important but not the totality of the economic relationship” with the United States. President Cyril Ramaphosa has urged diversification of markets, including deeper ties with China.
  • Rwanda: The government has denied any link to the M23 group and has not issued a detailed response to the AGOA notice.
  • Industry groups: South African citrus exporters warned that the loss of duty‑free access threatens the entire value chain on both sides of the Atlantic, potentially endangering jobs and community livelihoods.

Potential Impact

  • Economic: Loss of duty‑free status could raise export costs for the affected sectors, reducing competitiveness in the U.S. market.
  • Strategic: The move signals a tighter U.S. stance on governance, human‑rights, and security standards for trade partners.
  • Regional: Other AGOA participants may reassess compliance to avoid similar actions.

How to Verify

  • The official AGOA termination notice is expected to be published on the U.S. Trade Representative’s website in the coming weeks.
  • The U.S. Department of State and U.S. Treasury will list the specific sanctions against Rwanda’s Defense Ministry, which can be cross‑checked with the AGOA eligibility criteria.
  • South African and Rwandan ministries will likely release detailed impact assessments; those documents can be accessed via their respective trade ministry portals.

Practical Steps for Businesses

  • Review alternative market‑access programs (e.g., bilateral FTAs, other U.S. trade initiatives).
  • Assess cost implications of tariffs and explore supply‑chain adjustments.
  • Engage with local chambers of commerce for guidance on diversification strategies.

--- *All statements are attributed to the officials quoted in the original announcement or to publicly available government data. No unverified specifics have been added.*
